title: The lion and the hare
hookLine: a small hare outwits a lion with patience and wit (Masnavi 1)
tomorrow: where would you go to say goodbye to Rumi?

lines: A FACE IN THE DARK SCREEN.
cards: Lean over a still pond, or a dark phone screen, and a face looks back at you before you're ready for it. Rumi built a whole story in the Masnavi around that moment. A lion terrorizes the animals of a valley.
To stop the hunting, they strike a deal: every day, one of them will go to him on its own. Then it's the hare's turn. A lion, a hare, and a well.
How does the small one win?

teach.h: THE HARE ARRIVES LATE, ON PURPOSE.
teach.b: The hare takes its time. It arrives late, on purpose, and the lion is roaring with hunger and rage. The hare bows: forgive me.
I set out with a companion, but another lion stopped us on the road and took my friend. He says this valley is his. The lion is furious.
Show me this rival. The hare leads him to a deep well and steps back, trembling: he's down there.

The lion leans over the edge and looks into the water, and there is a lion, glaring up at him, with a hare beside it. He leaps at it, and the well takes him. The small one wins with patience and wit, not weight.
A version also sits in Kalila wa Dimna, a book of animal fables. Rumi turns it inward, and that's the part to feel. The rival in the well was the lion's own face.
Rumi says, paraphrased: many a fault you see in others is your own nature, showing in them. The lion attacked his reflection and drowned in it. So the hare's victory has two lessons.
Outside: weight isn't everything; a calm, clever mind can undo brute force. Inside: before you leap at the face glaring up at you, check whose face it is.

how: Sufi teachers use the lion and the hare both as a fable of wit over force and as a mirror: the faults we attack in others may be our own, reflected.

games.q: what does “the lion and the hare” mean?
o: running away from danger as fast as you can
a small animal's lucky escape from a big one
patience and wit that beat brute strength

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: a book of fables with this story

s: the hare beats the lion by being faster and stronger
patience and wit: it arrives late on purpose and leads him to the well.
in the story, the lion leaps at his own reflection
the rival in the well was his own face.
Rumi says many faults you see in others are your own nature showing in them
he turns the fable inward: check whose face it is before you leap.

games.q: a much bigger kid on your team keeps hogging the ball. shouting at him hasn't worked. what's the hare's way?
o: find a smart play that gets him passing, without a showdown.
shove back harder, and meet his weight with your weight.
quit the team, since the big ones always win anyway.
games.why: the hare didn't out-muscle the lion; it slowed down and thought. wit over weight.

practice: Fill a glass or bowl with water, or turn your phone screen dark, and look into it until your face settles there. Hold your gaze softly for the sit.
When an irritation with someone comes to mind, ask the face in the water, gently, whether some of it is yours.

wordCard.voice: The lion and the hare: Rumi's fable of a small hare that beats a lion with patience and wit, and a lion who leaps at his own reflection.

orig.note: Arabic: lion; the word for the lion of the fable.

carryVoice: Pocket this before the next showdown: wit over weight, and check the face in the well first. Seven of Rumi's eight.
